title: Replication, read replicas and failover
summary: Leader/follower replication, synchronous versus asynchronous, read replicas and their lag, read-your-writes, failing over without split brain, and why replicas are not backups: PITR, RPO and RTO.

steps.title: One leader, many followers
body: In **leader/follower** replication (primary/replica), every write goes to one primary. It records each
change in its write-ahead log (WAL) and streams the WAL to replicas, which replay it.
```text
writes                    WAL stream
app ───────────────> primary ═══════════════════> replica A  (same region, another AZ)
│ reads               ╚═══════════════════════> replica B  (reads only)
- **Asynchronous** (the default): the primary confirms the commit before any replica has it. Fast, but a
primary that dies loses whatever the replicas had not received.
- **Synchronous**: the commit waits until a standby confirms. In PostgreSQL: `synchronous_standby_names =
'ANY 1 (a, b)'` plus `synchronous_commit` (`on` waits for the standby's disk flush, `remote_apply` until
it is visible to reads there). No acknowledged write is lost, but every commit pays a round trip, and if
the standby is down the primary **stops committing** unless another standby can answer.
Managed "multi-AZ" databases usually keep a synchronous standby in a second AZ for failover, plus
asynchronous read replicas for scale.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: A commit is confirmed only after this replica has it
Receives changes after the commit is confirmed, so it can be behind
How far a replica's replayed state is behind the primary
Turning a replica into the new primary
Two nodes both accept writes as primary

steps.title: Read replicas and read-your-writes
body: Read replicas scale reads, not writes: every replica replays every write. They also serve **slightly old
data**. Lag is usually milliseconds, and grows to seconds or minutes when a replica is busy, a large
transaction replays, or the network is slow.
The classic bug: a user saves their profile (write to the primary), the page reloads (read from a
replica), and their change is gone. **Read-your-writes** consistency fixes it for that user without
sending everyone to the primary:
1. **Time window**: after a user writes, route their reads to the primary for a few seconds. Simple;
wrong when lag exceeds the window.
2. **Wait for the position**: after the write, remember `pg_current_wal_lsn()`. Read from a replica
only once its `pg_last_wal_replay_lsn()` has reached that position; otherwise use the primary. Exact.
Also watch **monotonic reads**: two reads by one user that hit two replicas with different lag can go
backwards in time. Pin a user (or a session) to one replica.

prompt: **Symptom first.** Support tickets: "I changed my delivery address, it saved, then the checkout page showed
the old one. A refresh later it was right." Writes go to the primary; all page reads go to two replicas.
code: SELECT application_name, state, replay_lag FROM pg_stat_replication;
options: Replica lag of about 2 s breaks read-your-writes; after a user writes, read their data from the primary until a replica has replayed their write
The write was lost; switch to synchronous replication everywhere
The replicas are broken; rebuild them
Add a third replica so the lag drops
steps.explain: The data was not lost, only not replayed yet. Two seconds is normal for a busy replica. Making every replica synchronous would slow every commit to fix a problem that only the writing user notices. Another replica does not reduce lag; it shares reads.

steps.prompt: The primary has written up to byte 5,000,000 of WAL, the replica has replayed up to 4,200,000, and it replays about 400,000 bytes per second. What does this print?
steps.explain: LSNs are byte positions in the WAL, so subtracting them gives the lag in bytes: `pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), replay_lsn)` on the primary. Dividing by the replay rate turns bytes into time.

steps.title: Failover without split brain
body: When the primary dies, a standby is **promoted** and writers are pointed at it. The hard part is being sure
the old primary is really gone. If it was only cut off by the network and comes back still accepting
writes, you have **split brain**: two primaries, two diverging histories, and a painful manual merge.
- **Detect by quorum**: an HA manager (Patroni with etcd, or the cloud provider's control plane) decides
with a majority of independent observers, never from one health check.
- **Fence the old primary** before promoting: stop it, cut its network, or make storage refuse it
(STONITH: "shoot the other node in the head"). Writers include a **fencing token** (an epoch number)
so a stale primary's writes are rejected.
- Promote the most up-to-date standby, then move the write endpoint (DNS name or proxy) to it.
Even managed failover takes tens of seconds to a couple of minutes, during which writes fail. Apps must
retry idempotent writes with backoff and reconnect, and must not cache the old primary's address forever.

steps.prompt: Put a safe failover in order.
lines: A majority of observers agree the primary is unreachable
Fence the old primary so it cannot accept writes
Promote the standby that has replayed the most WAL
Point the write endpoint at the new primary
Rebuild the old primary as a replica of the new one
steps.explain: Fencing before promotion is what prevents split brain. The old primary may have commits the new one never received, so it must be rewound or rebuilt (`pg_rewind`) rather than rejoined as it is.

steps.title: Replicas are not backups
body: A replica copies **everything**, including mistakes: `DROP TABLE orders` reaches every replica within
milliseconds. Backups protect against that.
- **PITR** (point-in-time recovery): a base backup plus the archived WAL since then lets you restore to any
moment, for example 14:31:59, one second before the bad migration. Tools: pgBackRest, WAL-G, Barman, or
the managed database's PITR setting.
- **RPO** (recovery point objective): how much data you may lose, measured in time. Async replication
failover loses about the replica lag; PITR loses whatever was not yet archived.
- **RTO** (recovery time objective): how long until service is back. A failover is minutes; restoring a
4 TB database from backup can be hours.
A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a backup. Schedule restore tests and time them: that
measured time is your real RTO.

steps.prompt: The primary takes 900 writes per second. Its asynchronous replica runs 2.5 s behind when the primary's disk fails and the replica is promoted. Roughly how many acknowledged writes are lost?
steps.explain: 900 writes/s × 2.5 s of lag = 2,250 writes that the primary confirmed and the replica never received. If that RPO is not acceptable, use a synchronous standby for failover, and keep async replicas for reads.

steps.title: A read-your-writes router
prompt: Write a class `ReplicaRouter` that decides whether a user's read may go to a replica.
- `void RecordWrite(string user, long lsn, long nowMs)`: the user's latest write ended at WAL position
`lsn` at time `nowMs` (a later write replaces the earlier one).
- `string RouteByLsn(string user, long replicaReplayLsn)`: `"primary"` if the user has a write the replica
has not replayed yet (its `lsn` is greater than `replicaReplayLsn`), else `"replica"`.
- `string RouteByTime(string user, long nowMs)`: `"primary"` if the user wrote less than `stickyMs` ago,
- `int PrimaryReads` and `int ReplicaReads`: how many reads each method has routed where.
Users who never wrote always read from the replica.
starter: public void RecordWrite(string user, long lsn, long nowMs) { }
public string RouteByLsn(string user, long replicaReplayLsn) => "replica";
public string RouteByTime(string user, long nowMs) => "replica";
solution: readonly Dictionary<string, (long Lsn, long AtMs)> lastWrite = new();
public int PrimaryReads { get; private set; }
public int ReplicaReads { get; private set; }
public void RecordWrite(string user, long lsn, long nowMs) => lastWrite[user] = (lsn, nowMs);
public string RouteByLsn(string user, long replicaReplayLsn) =>
Route(lastWrite.TryGetValue(user, out var w) && w.Lsn > replicaReplayLsn);
public string RouteByTime(string user, long nowMs) =>
Route(lastWrite.TryGetValue(user, out var w) && nowMs - w.AtMs < stickyMs);
hints: Keep one dictionary from user to `(Lsn, AtMs)` of their latest write.
Both routing methods compute a bool and pass it to one private helper that counts and returns the name.
template: Dojo.Eq("a user who never wrote reads from the replica", "replica", dojoR.RouteByLsn("ann", 100));
Dojo.Eq("the replica has not replayed ann's write", "primary", dojoR.RouteByLsn("ann", 450));
Dojo.Eq("once the replica reaches her LSN, it is safe", "replica", dojoR.RouteByLsn("ann", 500));
Dojo.Eq("other users are not affected", "replica", dojoR.RouteByLsn("bob", 450));
Dojo.Eq("inside the 2 s window: primary", "primary", dojoR.RouteByTime("ann", 11_000));
Dojo.Eq("reads routed to the primary", 3, dojoR.PrimaryReads);
Dojo.Eq("reads routed to the replica", 4, dojoR.ReplicaReads);
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("a negative window is rejected", () => new ReplicaRouter(-1));
explain: The LSN version is exact and costs one extra value per user (often kept in the session or a cookie). The
time version is a guess about lag: when a replica falls 5 s behind, a 2 s window serves stale reads
again. Seniors alert on `replay_lag` so that guess stays true.

steps.title: Build it: read replicas and lag
prompt: In the **System design board**, open *Read replicas and lag*. Personalised reads cannot be cached and the
primary is overloaded. Add read replicas from the app servers, size them so the primary has headroom,
and keep the replica lag under the goal, within the budget.
steps.explain: Watch the replica lag panel: replicas that are themselves near 100 % fall behind, because replaying writes competes with serving reads.
